subject: ss-rheumatology-immunology
title: Rheumatologic emergencies: key syndromes for NEET-PG and INI-CET

steps.tx: **Scleroderma renal crisis** is an emergency in systemic sclerosis, marked by sudden severe hypertension and rapidly falling kidney function. Vasospasm reduces renal perfusion and activates the renin-angiotensin system. Recent high-dose corticosteroid use is a documented risk factor. Early recognition matters because untreated disease carries very high one-year mortality.

steps.tx: The cornerstone of treatment is an **ACE inhibitor**, with captopril the classic short-acting agent used to titrate blood pressure safely. ACE inhibitors have transformed survival in this condition. If blood pressure stays above target on maximal dosing, a **dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker** is the appropriate add-on. Continue the ACE inhibitor even if dialysis is started, since some patients recover renal function.

steps.tx: **Antiphospholipid syndrome** requires a clinical event plus persistent laboratory positivity. Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I antibodies are the key tests. Confirm persistence on two occasions at least **12 weeks apart** to exclude transient antibodies. Warfarin with an INR of 2.0 to 3.0 is the standard long-term anticoagulant after a first venous thrombosis in definite APS.

steps.tx: **Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome** involves thrombosis in three or more organs within about a week, with small vessel occlusion. Surgery, infection and anticoagulation withdrawal are important triggers. Definite diagnosis needs histological confirmation plus laboratory evidence. Pregnancy-related management is different: no treatment is needed for positive antibodies alone, while a prior thrombosis or pregnancy loss calls for aspirin with or without heparin.
